docs.title: zig-tarantool
docs.text:
zig-tarantool lets you write Tarantool code in Zig. You can write stored procedures and Lua modules that run inside the Tarantool process, and programs that talk to Tarantool over the network.

Pre-release. The package has no versions yet: depend on it at a commit, and expect its API to change between commits.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Stored procedures in Zig. A plain Zig function becomes a language = 'C' function of Tarantool. Its arguments are decoded from MessagePack by the types of its parameters, its result is encoded back, and a Zig error it returns fails the call.
  • The box API in Zig. Spaces, indexes, tuples, transactions, sequences, fibers, channels, triggers, decimals and the logger, typed and with explicit lifetimes, over the C API of Tarantool (module.h).
  • Lua modules in Zig. A struct of Zig functions becomes a module that require() loads, with Lua values converted to Zig types and back.
  • A network client. An iproto connector for programs outside Tarantool: CRUD, calls, pipelined batches, the schema, watchers and interactive transactions. It runs over any std.Io, including one that makes a stored procedure yield its fiber while it waits for the network.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
A stored procedure:

const t = @import("tarantool");

fn add(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return a + b;
}

comptime {
    t.proc.exportProc("add", add);
}

built into hello.so and called from Tarantool:

box.schema.func.create('hello.add', { language = 'C' })
box.func['hello.add']:call({ 1, 2 }) -- 3

Your first module walks through it, from an empty directory to the call.

  • Concepts: the modules of the package, how Zig values map to MessagePack, who owns what, and how fibers yield.

  • Reference: the build helpers and steps, the API by module, the errors.
  • Project: how the package is tested, and what does not work yet.

The examples directory holds complete modules, each with a luatest suite that runs it against a live Tarantool.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
Tarantool stores tuples and passes arguments as MessagePack. The msgpack module encodes and decodes Zig values by their types, at compile time. The stored procedures, the box API and the client all go through it. This page lists what each Zig type becomes, and what decodes into it.

The rule is that nothing is guessed: a value of the wrong type is an error, never a conversion.

docs.title: Zig to MessagePack
docs.text:
Zig value MessagePack bool bool an integer type int, in the shortest form; a non-negative value of a signed type is written as unsigned, as Tarantool does f32, f64 float 64 []const u8, [N]u8, *const [N]u8 (a string literal) str msgpack.Bin{ .bytes = b } bin a slice or an array of anything else array a tuple struct, .{ a, b } array, the fields in order a named struct, struct { id: u64, name: []const u8 } map, the field names as keys ?T T, or nil for null void, null nil an enum its integer value msgpack.Value the value it holds msgpack.ext.Uuid, Datetime, Decimal, Interval, Ext the extension type of Tarantool, see Decimals and extensions tarantool.decimal.Decimal the decimal extension

A tuple of Tarantool is a MessagePack array, so a row or a key is a tuple struct: .{ 1, "alice" }, .{key}. A named struct encodes as a map, which is not a tuple. The functions that take a row, such as box.Typed(Row).put, encode the named struct Row as an array instead, the fields in their declaration order.

docs.title: MessagePack to Zig
docs.text:
msgpack.decode(T, &decoder) reads exactly one value into T:

Zig type Accepts Fails with bool bool NotBool an integer type int or uint that fits the type NotInt, Overflow f32, f64 float 32 or float 64 NotFloat []const u8 str NotStr msgpack.Bin bin NotBin [N]T an array of exactly N elements NotArray, ArityMismatch a tuple struct an array with one element per field NotArray, ArityMismatch a named struct a map whose keys are field names NotMap, UnknownField, MissingField ?T nil, as null, or what T accepts an enum its integer value msgpack.ext.Ext any extension NotExt

A few consequences:

  • An integer is not a float. Lua writes a number that has no fractional part as an integer, so box.func['m.f']:call({ 1 }) fails on an f64 parameter with NotFloat, and so does 1.0. A parameter that takes both needs the dynamic msgpack.Value, decoded in a raw procedure, see Stored procedures.
  • A string is not binary. A []const u8 takes a str only; a varbinary field of Tarantool is a bin and decodes into msgpack.Bin.
  • A named struct is strict. A key of the map that names no field is UnknownField. A field missing from the map is MissingField, unless it is optional, then it is null.
  • Slices other than strings do not decode. msgpack.decode allocates nothing, so it decodes fixed shapes only: []i64 is a compile error. For arrays of unknown length use msgpack.Value or walk the array with the Decoder.

docs.title: Borrowed strings
docs.text: Decoding allocates nothing: a decoded []const u8 is a slice of the input buffer. So a string decoded from a tuple lives as long as the tuple, and one decoded from a network reply lives until the next request on the connection. Lifetimes lists who owns each buffer, and the functions that copy for you.

docs.title: Dynamic values
docs.text:
msgpack.Value holds any MessagePack value:

pub const Value = union(enum) {
    nil,
    bool: bool,
    uint: u64,
    int: i64,
    float: f64,
    str: []const u8,
    bin: []const u8,
    array: []const Value,
    map: []const KV,
    ext: ext.Ext,
};

decoder.decodeValue(gpa) decodes into it; the arrays and maps are allocated with gpa, and msgpack.freeValue(gpa, value) frees them. The strings borrow the input, as above. Tuple.field(i, alloc) returns a field of a tuple as a Value.

docs.title: The codec on its own
docs.text:
const msgpack = @import("msgpack"); // or @import("tarantool").msgpack in a module

var buf = msgpack.Buffer.init(gpa);
defer buf.deinit();
try msgpack.encode(&buf, .{ 1, "alice", true });

var dec = msgpack.Decoder.init(buf.items());
const row = try msgpack.decode(struct { u64, []const u8, bool }, &dec);

msgpack.Buffer is a growable byte buffer; encode writes to anything with writeByte and writeAll. msgpack.encodeArray(w, value) writes any struct as an array, and msgpack.decodeArray(T, &dec) reads one into a named struct.

A struct can define its own encoding: if it declares pub fn mpEncode(self, w: anytype) !void and pub fn mpDecode(dec: *msgpack.Decoder) msgpack.DecodeError!Self, encode and decode call them. tarantool.decimal.Decimal uses this.

docs.title: Fibers and yields
docs.text: Tarantool runs the requests of its users in fibers: coroutines on a single thread, the TX thread, that switch only when one of them yields. A stored procedure runs in the fiber of its request. This page says what that means for Zig code, and which calls of the SDK yield.

docs.title: One thread, cooperative switching
docs.text:
While a procedure runs and does not yield, no other request of the instance runs. That makes code between two yields atomic with respect to the other fibers. It also means that a procedure that computes for a second, or blocks in a system call, stalls the whole instance for that second.

So in a module:

  • Do not block the thread. std.Thread.sleep, a blocking read of a socket, a std.Io.Threaded network call: each of them stops every fiber. Use the fiber versions: fiber.sleep, coio.wait, fiberio.io().
  • Offload what has to block. coio.call(Ctx, func, &ctx) runs func on a worker thread of Tarantool and yields the fiber until it returns. func must not touch the box, the region, fibers or Lua: none of them are thread-safe.
  • Assume a yield invalidates what you read. After a yield, other fibers may have changed the spaces. Read again, or do the work in a transaction.

docs.title: What yields
docs.text:
Call Yields fiber.sleep, fiber.yield, fiber.reschedule always fiber.spawn, spawnWithAttr, spawnDetached yes: the new fiber runs first, until its first yield Fiber.join until the fiber ends cond.Cond.wait, waitTimeout, waitUntil until a signal or the timeout latch.Latch.lock when the latch is held fiber.Channel.send, recv when the channel is full, or empty coio.wait, coio.call, coio.getAddrInfo yes every network operation over fiberio.io() while it waits for the socket info.waitRo until the state changes or the timeout a commit of a transaction while the write-ahead log is written, unless the engine has nothing to write Space and Index operations on memtx no

A yield inside a transaction matters: memtx aborts a transaction that yields, unless the instance runs the MVCC engine (memtx_use_mvcc_engine = true). See Transactions.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text: Fiber.cancel asks a fiber to stop; it does not stop it. The fiber sees the request at its next yield: the waits of the SDK return error.Cancelled, and fiber.isCancelled() turns true. A fiber body that loops without waiting should check fiber.isCancelled() itself.

docs.title: Network I/O from a fiber
docs.text:
tarantool.fiberio.io() is a std.Io whose network operations do not block the thread. A socket is non-blocking; when a read or a write would block, the fiber waits in coio.wait and Tarantool runs other fibers until the socket is ready. The network client takes a std.Io, so with this one it runs inside a stored procedure:

var conn = try client.Connection.connect(gpa, t.fiberio.io(), .{ .address = uri });

Only the operations the client needs are implemented: connecting to an IP address, reading, writing and closing a socket. The rest of std.Io, such as files, timers and async, panics with the name of the operation. See The client in a stored procedure.

docs.title: Modules and layers
docs.text: zig-tarantool is four Zig modules in one package. Inside them, every typed API sits on a raw one that you can use directly. This page describes both structures.

docs.title: The four modules
docs.text:
Module Imports What it is msgpack std The MessagePack codec. It has no Tarantool dependency. tarantool-proto msgpack The protocol types that do not depend on where the code runs: iterator types, select options, update operations, the iproto constants. tarantool msgpack, tarantool-proto, the C API of Tarantool The in-process SDK: everything a module does inside Tarantool. tarantool-client msgpack, tarantool-proto The iproto network client.

The imports only go down the table. tarantool-client cannot import tarantool, because the build does not give it that import. So the client compiles and runs in a program that has no Tarantool to resolve the box_* symbols against. zig build purity checks this: it compiles a module that crosses the boundary and expects the compilation to fail.

A module built with addModule can import all four. A program built with addExecutable gets every module except tarantool.

The SDK re-exports what it shares with the other modules, so a module only needs @import("tarantool"):

Name in tarantool Is tarantool.msgpack the msgpack module tarantool.query tarantool-proto's query: IteratorType, SelectOptions tarantool.update tarantool-proto's update: update operations

A module that runs the network client inside Tarantool also imports tarantool-client, see The client in a stored procedure.

docs.title: How a module reaches Tarantool
docs.text:
A module is a shared library with undefined symbols: box_insert, fiber_new, lua_pushnil, and the rest of the C API of Tarantool. The library is not linked against Tarantool. Tarantool exports these symbols from its own executable, and the dynamic loader binds them when Tarantool loads the module with dlopen.

So:

  • A module builds without Tarantool installed, and cross-compiles: zig build -Dtarget=aarch64-macos makes a .dylib on Linux.
  • A module loads only into a Tarantool that exports every symbol it uses. That is 3.5 or later, see Install.
  • A missing symbol shows when Tarantool loads the module: at the first call of one of its functions, or at require. It does not show at build time.

tarantool.c declares the C API by hand, in Zig: the functions, the opaque types, the constants. Every Tarantool symbol the SDK uses is declared there. zig build verify-cabi -Dverify-cabi=true translates the real module.h and compares every declaration with it, see Testing.

docs.title: Raw and typed layers
docs.text:
Each part of the SDK has a raw layer that maps the C API one to one, and a typed layer built only from the raw one. You can drop to the raw layer whenever the typed one does not fit.

Area Raw Typed Stored procedures fn(ctx, args, args_end) callconv(.c) c_int, proc.returnValue, proc.exportRaw proc.exportProc(name, f) with a plain Zig f Data box.Space, box.Index, box.Tuple, Index.iterator box.Typed(Row), Index.range(Row, ...), Index.top Lua functions a lua_CFunction over lua.Lua a plain Zig function in lua.exportModule Client requests callRaw, insertRaw, ... over pre-encoded MessagePack call, insert, ... over Zig values Anything else tarantool.c, the C API itself

The typed layers add no parsing of their own: they encode and decode through msgpack, and call the raw layer.

docs.title: Hidden symbols
docs.text:
Some functions of Tarantool are not in its public C API. They are compiled into the executable, but they are not exported, so dlsym does not find them. tarantool.symresolve.resolve(name) finds such a symbol: it reads the full symbol table of the executable, .symtab on Linux and LC_SYMTAB on macOS. You then cast the pointer to the type of the function.

It is an escape hatch. The internal functions of Tarantool change between versions without notice, and a stripped executable has no symbol table at all. See Introspection.

docs.title: Lifetimes
docs.text: Zig has no garbage collector, and Tarantool owns much of the memory that a module touches: tuples, the fiber region, the error of the last call. This page says who owns each buffer, how long it lives, and which functions copy for you.

docs.title: Tuples
docs.text:
A tuple is memory of Tarantool, counted by references. A box.Tuple holds one reference, and deinit releases it.

  • A tuple returned by a read or a write is yours. Space.get, insert, replace, delete, update, Index.get, min, max, random, Iterator.next and Index.select hand back tuples with a reference you own. Call deinit once you are done:
if (try space.get(.{key})) |row| {
    defer row.deinit();
    // read row here
}

  • A tuple you do not need is still yours. replace returns the stored tuple, so _ = try space.replace(...) leaks a reference. Release it, or use the *Discard variant, which runs the same operation and releases the result: insertDiscard, replaceDiscard, deleteDiscard, updateDiscard, upsertDiscard.

  • A tuple from a Cursor is borrowed. Index.cursor yields tuples it releases itself, at the next next or at deinit. Copy out what must outlive that.

  • A string read from a tuple is a slice of the tuple. Tuple.get(i, []const u8, alloc), Tuple.decode and Tuple.decodeRow return slices into the tuple's data; they are valid while you hold the tuple. dupe them to keep them longer.

The typed functions copy for you: box.Typed(Row).get, Range(Row).next and Index.top copy every string field of the row into the allocator you pass, and release the tuple before they return. Typed(Row).free, Range(Row).free and Range(Row).freeSlice free those copies.

docs.title: The fiber region
docs.text:
The region is a per-fiber stack of scratch memory in Tarantool. tarantool.region.allocator() allocates on it; its free does nothing. Tarantool reclaims the region of a stored procedure when the call ends, so memory a procedure allocates there needs no free, and a procedure may return a string that lives there:

fn greet(name: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    return std.fmt.allocPrint(t.region.allocator(), "Hello, {s}!", .{name});
}

A loop that allocates on the region on each step grows it until the call ends. region.Savepoint gives the memory back earlier:

for (keys) |key| {
    const svp = t.region.Savepoint.save();
    defer svp.restore(); // everything allocated on the region since save()
    const scratch = try t.region.allocator().alloc(u8, 4096);
    _ = scratch;
    _ = key;
}

The box operations encode their arguments on the region under a savepoint of their own, and restore it before they return. A function that takes an allocator and may be given the region, such as Tuple.new(values, alloc), takes no savepoint: if you pass region.allocator(), the savepoint is yours.

A fiber you spawn has a region of its own, which Tarantool frees when the fiber ends. In a fiber that runs for long, bound every use of the region with a savepoint.

docs.title: Arguments of a stored procedure
docs.text:
The arguments of a call are a buffer of Tarantool that lives until the call returns. A typed procedure's []const u8 parameters are slices of it: use them during the call, and copy what you store elsewhere. Storing it in a space copies it, so space.replace(.{ key, value }) needs no copy.

A Lua function made by lua.exportModule gets its []const u8 arguments copied to the region, because a Lua string lives only while it is on the Lua stack.

docs.title: Errors of Tarantool
docs.text: When a box operation fails, it returns error.BoxOp, and the message is in the error of the fiber, in Tarantool: tarantool.err.lastError() points to it. That pointer is valid until the next box call replaces the error. err.lastMessage(&buf) copies the message into a buffer of yours.

docs.title: Fiber objects
docs.text:
fiber.Channel, cond.Cond, latch.Latch and fiber.FiberAttr own memory of Tarantool and free it in deinit. Free them only when no fiber waits on them: join the fibers that use a channel before its deinit. In a debug build, Channel.deinit and Latch.deinit check this and panic.

A fiber.Fiber(T) handle owns the result slot of the fiber, which join frees. Join it exactly once.

docs.title: The network client
docs.text:
A connection reads each reply into its own buffer, and decoded values borrow it:

  • A []const u8 in the result of call, eval, get, insert, select and the rest is valid until the next request on the same connection.
  • select returns a slice you free with the allocator you passed; the strings in its rows still borrow the connection's buffer.
  • The results of a Batch live in the batch, until its deinit.
  • A watcher event lives until the next waitEvent or pollEvent.

Copy what must live longer, as the proxy example does before it closes its connection:

const row = try conn.space("kv").get(.{key}, struct { []const u8, []const u8 }) orelse return null;
return try t.region.allocator().dupe(u8, row[1]);

conn.last_error belongs to the connection until the next error or close.

docs.title: Your first client
docs.text:
This page writes a Zig program that connects to Tarantool over the network and calls the stored procedure of Your first module. It extends the hello project of that page.

A client program does not run inside Tarantool and does not import tarantool: it imports tarantool-client, the iproto connector of the package.

docs.title: Start a server
docs.text:
The server serves hello.add to the guest user on port 3301.

server.lua:

local ext = require('tarantool').build.mod_format
package.cpath = 'zig-out/lib/?.' .. ext .. ';' .. package.cpath

require('fio').mktree('data')
box.cfg{ memtx_dir = 'data', wal_dir = 'data', listen = '127.0.0.1:3301' }

box.schema.func.create('hello.add', { language = 'C', if_not_exists = true })
box.schema.func.create('hello.greet', { language = 'C', if_not_exists = true })
box.schema.user.grant('guest', 'execute', 'function', 'hello.add', { if_not_exists = true })

$ tarantool server.lua

The server keeps running; use another terminal for the rest.

docs.title: Write the program
docs.text:
src/client.zig:

//! Connect to 127.0.0.1:3301 as guest, call hello.add, and show what a denied
//! call looks like.

const std = @import("std");
const client = @import("tarantool-client");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var conn = try client.Connection.connect(init.gpa, init.io, .{
        .address = "127.0.0.1:3301",
    });
    defer conn.close();

    try conn.ping();

    const sum = try conn.call("hello.add", .{ 1, 2 }, i64);
    std.debug.print("hello.add(1, 2) = {d}\n", .{sum});

    // The guest may not call hello.greet: the server answers with an error,
    // which the connection keeps in last_error.
    if (conn.call("hello.greet", .{"Zig"}, []const u8)) |_| {
        unreachable;
    } else |err| switch (err) {
        error.ServerError => std.debug.print("hello.greet: {s}\n", .{conn.last_error.?.message}),
        else => return err,
    }
}
  • Connection.connect(gpa, io, options) opens a TCP connection, reads the greeting and logs in. The address is host:port with a numeric IP. With no .user, it logs in as guest, and a guest with no password skips the authentication request.
  • io is the std.Io the connection does its network operations through. init.io is the one main gets from the Zig runtime. Inside a stored procedure, the package offers one that yields the fiber instead, see The client in a stored procedure.
  • call(name, args, Result) encodes args as the argument array and decodes the value the function returns into Result.
  • A request the server refuses fails with error.ServerError; conn.last_error holds its code and message until the next error.

docs.title: Build and run it
docs.text:
Add the program to build.zig, after the module:

    const cli = tarantool.addExecutable(b, .{
        .name = "hello-client",
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/client.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    b.installArtifact(cli);

addExecutable makes a program that can import tarantool-client, but not tarantool: the in-process API needs a Tarantool to run in. A program installs as usual, with b.installArtifact.

$ zig build
$ ./zig-out/bin/hello-client
hello.add(1, 2) = 3
hello.greet: Execute access to function 'hello.greet' is denied for user 'guest'

docs.title: Your first module
docs.text:
This page builds a Tarantool module with two stored procedures, loads it into Tarantool and calls them. It needs Zig and Tarantool, see Install.

A module is a shared library that Tarantool loads: hello.so on Linux, hello.dylib on macOS. Each stored procedure of the module is a C symbol in it, and Tarantool calls it as the function hello.<symbol>.

docs.title: Set up the project
docs.text:
mkdir hello && cd hello
zig init --minimal
zig fetch --save git+https://github.com/tarantool-contrib/zig-tarantool#<commit>
mkdir src

zig fetch adds the package to build.zig.zon as tarantool; a checkout works as well, see Install.

docs.title: Write the procedures
docs.text:
src/hello.zig:

//! hello.add(a, b) and hello.greet(name): two typed stored procedures.

const std = @import("std");
const t = @import("tarantool");

/// hello.add(a, b) -> a + b
fn add(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return a + b;
}

/// hello.greet(name) -> 'Hello, <name>!', or the error EmptyName.
fn greet(name: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    if (name.len == 0) return error.EmptyName;
    return std.fmt.allocPrint(t.region.allocator(), "Hello, {s}!", .{name});
}

comptime {
    t.proc.exportProc("add", add);
    t.proc.exportProc("greet", greet);
}

exportProc(name, f) exports the C symbol name, a function that Tarantool can call. It decodes the arguments of the call into the parameters of f by their types, calls f, and encodes its result back. Here:

  • add takes two integers. A call with one argument, or with a string, fails with an error and never reaches add.
  • greet takes a string and returns a string or an error. A Zig error fails the call, with the name of the error as its message.
  • The greeting is allocated on the fiber region, t.region.allocator(): scratch memory that Tarantool reclaims when the call ends. There is nothing to free.

Stored procedures covers the types a procedure takes and returns.

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
build.zig:

const std = @import("std");
const tarantool = @import("tarantool");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    const hello = tarantool.addModule(b, .{
        .name = "hello",
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/hello.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    tarantool.installModule(b, hello);
}

$ zig build
$ ls zig-out/lib
hello.so

addModule makes a shared library that can import tarantool, with the box_* symbols left for Tarantool to resolve. installModule installs it under the name Tarantool looks for: hello.so, or hello.dylib on macOS, without the lib prefix that b.installArtifact would add. See Build reference.

docs.title: Call it from Tarantool
docs.text:
init.lua:

-- Find zig-out/lib/hello.so (hello.dylib on macOS).
local ext = require('tarantool').build.mod_format
package.cpath = 'zig-out/lib/?.' .. ext .. ';' .. package.cpath

require('fio').mktree('data')
box.cfg{ memtx_dir = 'data', wal_dir = 'data' }

box.schema.func.create('hello.add', { language = 'C', if_not_exists = true })
box.schema.func.create('hello.greet', { language = 'C', if_not_exists = true })

print(box.func['hello.add']:call({ 1, 2 }))
print(box.func['hello.greet']:call({ 'Zig' }))
print(pcall(box.func['hello.greet'].call, box.func['hello.greet'], { '' }))

os.exit(0)

$ tarantool init.lua
3
Hello, Zig!
false   EmptyName

box.schema.func.create('hello.add', {language = 'C'}) declares a function whose code is the symbol add of the module hello. On the first call Tarantool finds hello.so on package.cpath, loads it and resolves the symbol. require('tarantool').build.mod_format is the extension Tarantool looks for, so or dylib.

The function is in the schema now, so it is also callable over the network. Your first client calls it from a Zig program.

docs.title: Your first modules with tt
docs.text:
This page builds a Zig module as part of a tt package: tt runs zig build, puts the module into .rocks/ of the project, runs Tarantool with it and runs its tests. The module holds two stored procedures and a Lua module. Your first module builds the same kind of module with Zig and Tarantool alone.

It needs Zig, see Install, and tt 3 with the zig build backend: tt version --modules lists the module build in a tt that has it. tt installs Tarantool into the project itself.

docs.title: Create the project
docs.text:
$ mkdir myapp && cd myapp
$ git init
$ tt new
created /home/me/myapp/app.manifest.toml for package myapp
$ tt binary install tarantool

tt new writes app.manifest.toml, the manifest of the package myapp. tt binary install tarantool installs the latest Tarantool into .tarantool/ of the project; the commands of tt below run that one.

docs.title: Set up the component
docs.text:
The Zig code of the package is a component: a directory with its own Zig project. Create it in libs/hello/ and add zig-tarantool to it:

mkdir -p libs/hello/src && cd libs/hello
zig init --minimal
zig fetch --save git+https://github.com/tarantool-contrib/zig-tarantool#<commit>
cd ../..

zig fetch adds the package to libs/hello/build.zig.zon as tarantool; a checkout works as well, see Using with tt.

docs.title: Write the module
docs.text:
libs/hello/src/hello.zig:

//! The module hello of the package myapp: two stored procedures and a Lua
//! module.

const std = @import("std");
const t = @import("tarantool");

/// The stored procedure myapp.hello.add(a, b) -> a + b.
fn add(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return a + b;
}

/// The stored procedure myapp.hello.greet(name) -> 'Hello, <name>!', or the
/// error EmptyName.
fn greet(name: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    if (name.len == 0) return error.EmptyName;
    return std.fmt.allocPrint(t.region.allocator(), "Hello, {s}!", .{name});
}

/// mul(a, b) of the Lua module require('myapp.hello').
fn mul(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return a * b;
}

comptime {
    t.proc.exportProc("add", add);
    t.proc.exportProc("greet", greet);
    t.lua.exportModule("myapp_hello", .{ .mul = mul });
}

One library is two modules for Tarantool:

  • a C module: add and greet are the C symbols of the stored procedures myapp.hello.add and myapp.hello.greet, see Stored procedures;
  • a Lua module: exportModule("myapp_hello", ...) exports luaopen_myapp_hello, which require('myapp.hello') calls, see Lua modules.

The names have the namespace of the package, myapp, in front, because tt installs the module as myapp/hello.so.

libs/hello/build.zig:

const std = @import("std");
const tarantool = @import("tarantool");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    const hello = tarantool.addModule(b, .{
        .name = "hello",
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/hello.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    tarantool.installModule(b, hello);
}

This is the build.zig of Your first module: installModule installs lib/hello.so, or lib/hello.dylib on macOS, where tt takes it from.

docs.title: Declare the component
docs.text:
Add the component to app.manifest.toml:

[components.hello]
path = "libs/hello"
exclude = ["zig-pkg/**"]

[components.hello.build]
backend = "zig"
module = "hello"
  • backend = "zig" builds the component with zig build, and module = "hello" is the module the build installs.
  • exclude keeps zig-pkg/ out of the package. Zig fetches the dependencies of build.zig.zon there, next to it, and tt lays out the *.lua files of a component into the package, those of the dependencies among them.

Zig and tt leave files that git does not need to keep:

$ printf '.rocks/\n.tarantool/\n.env/\n_build/\nzig-out/\nzig-pkg/\n.zig-cache/\n' > .gitignore

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
$ tt package build
$ find .rocks/lib -name 'hello*'
.rocks/lib/tarantool/myapp/hello.so

tt package build runs zig build in libs/hello/, in the ReleaseSafe mode, and copies the module into .rocks/lib/tarantool/myapp/. Tarantool looks for modules in .rocks/ of its current directory, so the code of the project loads it with no package.cpath.

The first build compiles zig-tarantool and takes a while; the next ones reuse the cache of zig in _build/.

docs.title: Call the Lua module
docs.text:
$ tt run -e "print(require('myapp.hello').mul(6, 7))" - </dev/null
42

tt run runs the Tarantool of the project with the arguments as given. require('myapp.hello') finds myapp/hello.so in .rocks/ and calls its luaopen_myapp_hello.

docs.title: Call the stored procedures
docs.text:
app.lua:

require('fio').mktree('data')
box.cfg({memtx_dir = 'data', wal_dir = 'data'})

box.schema.func.create('myapp.hello.add', {language = 'C', if_not_exists = true})
box.schema.func.create('myapp.hello.greet', {language = 'C', if_not_exists = true})

print(box.func['myapp.hello.add']:call({1, 2}))
print(box.func['myapp.hello.greet']:call({'tt'}))
print(pcall(box.func['myapp.hello.greet'].call, box.func['myapp.hello.greet'], {''}))

os.exit(0)

$ tt run app.lua
3
Hello, tt!
false   EmptyName

The log of box.cfg goes to the standard error, around these lines. box.schema.func.create('myapp.hello.add', {language = 'C'}) declares a function whose code is the symbol add of the module myapp.hello: Tarantool takes the module from the name up to its last dot and the symbol from the rest.

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
$ tt package add luatest --dev
added luatest * to [dev_dependencies]
  checks 3.4.1-1
  luatest 1.4.5-1

test/hello_test.lua:

local t = require('luatest')
local fio = require('fio')
local hello = require('myapp.hello')

local g = t.group()

g.before_all(function()
    local dir = fio.tempdir()
    box.cfg({memtx_dir = dir, wal_dir = dir})
    box.schema.func.create('myapp.hello.add', {language = 'C', if_not_exists = true})
    box.schema.func.create('myapp.hello.greet', {language = 'C', if_not_exists = true})
end)

g.test_mul = function()
    t.assert_equals(hello.mul(6, 7), 42)
end

g.test_add = function()
    t.assert_equals(box.func['myapp.hello.add']:call({1, 2}), 3)
end

g.test_greet = function()
    t.assert_equals(box.func['myapp.hello.greet']:call({'tt'}), 'Hello, tt!')
    t.assert_error_msg_equals('EmptyName', box.func['myapp.hello.greet'].call,
        box.func['myapp.hello.greet'], {''})
end

$ tt test
...
Ran 3 tests in 0.047 seconds, 3 succeeded, 0 failed

tt test builds the package first, so a change of the Zig code is in the module the tests load. luatest runs the tests in a Tarantool of its own, which the group configures in before_all. Leave log out of that box.cfg: luatest has set it already, and box.cfg cannot change it.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: This page lists what zig-tarantool needs and adds it to a Zig project.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
What Version Needed for Zig 0.17.1 everything; the package pins it in build.zig.zon and .zig-version Tarantool 3.5 or later loading the modules you build Tarantool 3.0 or later the server a client program talks to luatest any only the test suite of this repository

A module needs Tarantool 3.5 because it calls box_* functions that older Tarantool does not export, such as box_tuple_data and box_status (3.3 and 3.4 lack them, 3.0 lacks more). Tarantool resolves these symbols when it loads the module, so on an older version the load fails with an undefined symbol. A client program only speaks the protocol, and 3.0 is the first version with the features it requires.

Platforms:

Platform CI Linux x86_64 runs the suite against Tarantool 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8 and 3.9 Linux arm64 runs the suite against Tarantool 3.5 and 3.9 macOS, Apple silicon runs the suite against the Tarantool of Homebrew macOS, Intel builds the modules and programs, does not run them

docs.title: Install Zig
docs.text:
Take Zig 0.17.1 from ziglang.org/download and put it on PATH:

$ zig version
0.17.1

docs.title: Install Tarantool
docs.text:
Install Tarantool 3.5 or later from tarantool.io/download; on macOS, brew install tarantool. Or run it in Docker:

$ docker run --rm -it tarantool/tarantool:3.9

The modules do not need the Tarantool headers to build: the package carries its own declarations of the C API. The headers are only needed to check those declarations, see Testing.

docs.title: Add the package to a project
docs.text:
Create a project, if you have none yet:

mkdir hello && cd hello
zig init --minimal

and add zig-tarantool to its build.zig.zon under the name tarantool. Its build.zig exports the helpers that build modules and programs, and they find the package by that name.

At a commit of the repository:

zig fetch --save git+https://github.com/tarantool-contrib/zig-tarantool#<commit>

zig fetch downloads the package, computes its hash and writes both to build.zig.zon:

.dependencies = .{
    .tarantool = .{
        .url = "git+https://github.com/tarantool-contrib/zig-tarantool#<commit>",
        .hash = "tarantool-0.0.0-...",
    },
},

Or from a checkout next to the project, which is handy while you change both:

.dependencies = .{
    .tarantool = .{ .path = "../zig-tarantool" },
},

A .path dependency has no hash: Zig builds the checkout as it is.
