docs.title: Transactions
docs.text: This page makes several writes of a stored procedure atomic: a transaction that commits when the code succeeds and rolls back when it fails, savepoints inside it, its options, and code that runs at the commit. The module is ledger, over a space of accounts.

docs.title: The module
docs.text:
local accounts = box.schema.space.create('accounts', {
    if_not_exists = true,
    format = { { name = 'id', type = 'string' }, { name = 'balance', type = 'integer' } },
})
accounts:create_index('pk', { parts = { 'id' }, if_not_exists = true })

src/ledger.zig:

//! ledger: transfers between accounts {id, balance}, all or nothing.

const std = @import("std");
const t = @import("tarantool");
const box = t.box;
const txn = t.txn;
const update = t.update;

/// Add `amount` to the balance of `id`; fail if it goes below zero.
fn credit(id: []const u8, amount: i64) !void {
    const accounts = try box.Space.byName("accounts");
    const row = (try accounts.update(.{id}, .{update.add(1, amount)})) orelse return error.NoAccount;
    defer row.deinit();
    if ((try row.get(1, i64, std.heap.c_allocator)).? < 0) return error.Overdraft;
}

fn move(from: []const u8, to: []const u8, amount: i64) !void {
    try credit(from, -amount);
    try credit(to, amount);
}

/// Commits so far. Static: the trigger runs after the procedure returned.
var commits: u64 = 0;

fn countCommit(counter: *u64) void {
    counter.* += 1;
}

fn transferTx(from: []const u8, to: []const u8, amount: i64) !void {
    try t.trigger.onCommit(&commits, countCommit);
    try move(from, to, amount);
}

/// ledger.transfer(from, to, amount): both writes, or none.
fn transfer(from: []const u8, to: []const u8, amount: i64) !void {
    try txn.transaction(transferTx, .{ from, to, amount });
}

fn splitTx(from: []const u8, a: []const u8, b: []const u8, amount: i64) !u32 {
    try t.trigger.onCommit(&commits, countCommit);
    var paid: u32 = 0;
    for ([_][]const u8{ a, b }) |to| {
        const svp = try txn.Savepoint.save();
        move(from, to, amount) catch |e| switch (e) {
            error.NoAccount, error.Overdraft => {
                try svp.rollback(); // undo this payment only
                continue;
            },
            else => return e,
        };
        paid += 1;
    }
    return paid;
}

/// ledger.split(from, a, b, amount) -> how many of the two payments were made.
fn split(from: []const u8, a: []const u8, b: []const u8, amount: i64) !u32 {
    return txn.transaction(splitTx, .{ from, a, b, amount });
}

/// ledger.transfer_within(from, to, amount, seconds): a transfer that rolls
/// back if it takes longer than `seconds`.
fn transferWithin(from: []const u8, to: []const u8, amount: i64, seconds: f64) !void {
    try txn.transactionWith(.{ .timeout = seconds }, move, .{ from, to, amount });
}

/// ledger.commits() -> the number of transactions of this module committed.
fn getCommits() u64 {
    return commits;
}

comptime {
    t.proc.exportProc("transfer", transfer);
    t.proc.exportProc("split", split);
    t.proc.exportProc("transfer_within", transferWithin);
    t.proc.exportProc("commits", getCommits);
}

for _, name in ipairs({ 'transfer', 'split', 'transfer_within', 'commits' }) do
    box.schema.func.create('ledger.' .. name, { language = 'C', if_not_exists = true })
end
local function call(name, ...)
    return box.func['ledger.' .. name]:call({ ... })
end
accounts:replace({ 'alice', 100 })
accounts:replace({ 'bob', 0 })

call('transfer', 'alice', 'bob', 30)
accounts:get('alice')[2]                 -- 70
call('transfer', 'alice', 'nobody', 10)  -- error: NoAccount
accounts:get('alice')[2]                 -- 70: the debit was rolled back
call('split', 'alice', 'bob', 'nobody', 20) -- 1
accounts:get('alice')[2]                 -- 50
call('transfer_within', 'alice', 'bob', 5, 1.5)
call('commits')                          -- 2

docs.title: Run code in a transaction
docs.text:
txn.transaction(f, args) begins a transaction, calls f with the tuple args, and:

  • commits, and returns what f returned, when f succeeds;
  • rolls back, and returns the error, when f returns one.

f may return a value, void, or an error union of either. The second transfer above fails at the credit of nobody, after the debit of alice; the rollback undoes the debit.

A transaction is bound to the fiber. Calling transaction while one is active fails, as box.begin() does: txn.active() tells whether there is one, and txn.id() gives its id.

docs.title: Savepoints
docs.text:
txn.Savepoint.save() marks a point in the active transaction; svp.rollback() undoes what the transaction did after it, and the transaction goes on. split uses one per payment, so a failed payment does not undo the one before it.

rollback fails with error.StaleSavepoint when the transaction it was saved in has ended. The savepoints of a transaction need no free: Tarantool frees them with the transaction.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
txn.transactionWith(options, f, args) applies options before f runs:

Option Does .isolation the isolation level: .read_committed, .read_confirmed, .best_effort, .linearizable; .default keeps the one of box.cfg .timeout seconds after which Tarantool rolls the transaction back .sync makes the commit wait for the quorum of synchronous replication

They are the options of box.begin(). The isolation levels take effect with the MVCC engine, see below. Outside transactionWith, txn.setIsolation, txn.setTimeout and txn.makeSync set them on the active transaction; the isolation only before its first write.

docs.title: Yields in a transaction
docs.text:
memtx without MVCC aborts a transaction that yields: the next write, or the commit, fails with Transaction has been aborted by a fiber yield. A transaction of a module must not sleep, wait on a channel or do network I/O, unless the instance runs with

box.cfg{ memtx_use_mvcc_engine = true }

which allows yields and makes the isolation levels work. Fibers and yields lists what yields.

docs.title: Code at commit and rollback
docs.text:
trigger.onCommit(context, f) runs f(context) once, after the active transaction commits; trigger.onRollback(context, f) once, if it rolls back. Outside a transaction they fail with error.NoTxn.

  • f returns nothing and cannot fail: the commit has happened.
  • f must not yield.
  • context is a pointer, and it must stay valid until the transaction ends, which may be after the procedure returned. A variable on the stack of the procedure is not: use a global, as commits above, or memory you free in f.

The failed transfer above registered its trigger, then rolled back, so the trigger did not run: commits counts the first transfer and the split. The transfer_within call does not register one.

docs.title: Memory of a transaction
docs.text: txn.alloc(T) and txn.allocSlice(T, n) allocate on the memory of the active transaction, which Tarantool frees when the transaction ends. There is no free.

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text: A module can run code when something happens in Tarantool: a write to a space, the commit or the rollback of a transaction, the shutdown of the server. tarantool.trigger registers Zig functions for these. This page writes a module that audits a space and rejects some writes.

docs.title: The module
docs.text:
src/audit.zig:

//! audit: count the writes to a space, and reject a negative quantity.

const std = @import("std");
const t = @import("tarantool");
const trigger = t.trigger;

const Audit = struct {
    inserts: u64 = 0,
    replaces: u64 = 0,
    updates: u64 = 0,
    deletes: u64 = 0,
    handle: ?trigger.SpaceTrigger = null,
};

/// Global: a trigger outlives the call that registers it.
var audit: Audit = .{};

fn onReplace(a: *Audit, event: trigger.ReplaceEvent) !void {
    if (event.new) |row| {
        const qty = (try row.get(1, i64, std.heap.c_allocator)) orelse 0;
        if (qty < 0) return error.NegativeQty; // rejects the write
    }
    switch (event.op) {
        .insert => a.inserts += 1,
        .replace => a.replaces += 1,
        .update => a.updates += 1,
        .delete => a.deletes += 1,
        .upsert => {},
    }
}

fn onShutdown(a: *Audit) void {
    t.say.info("audit: {d} inserts, {d} deletes", .{ a.inserts, a.deletes });
}

/// audit.enable(space): start auditing a space.
fn enable(space: []const u8) !void {
    if (audit.handle != null) return error.AlreadyEnabled;
    const s = try t.box.Space.byName(space);
    audit.handle = try trigger.onReplace(s.id, &audit, onReplace);
    try trigger.onShutdown(&audit, onShutdown);
}

/// audit.disable(): stop.
fn disable() !void {
    const handle = audit.handle orelse return error.NotEnabled;
    audit.handle = null;
    try handle.remove();
    try trigger.removeShutdown(&audit, onShutdown);
}

/// audit.counts() -> {inserts = , replaces = , updates = , deletes = }
fn counts() struct { inserts: u64, replaces: u64, updates: u64, deletes: u64 } {
    return .{ .inserts = audit.inserts, .replaces = audit.replaces, .updates = audit.updates, .deletes = audit.deletes };
}

comptime {
    t.proc.exportProc("enable", enable);
    t.proc.exportProc("disable", disable);
    t.proc.exportProc("counts", counts);
}

local stock = box.schema.space.create('stock', { if_not_exists = true })
stock:create_index('pk', { if_not_exists = true })
for _, name in ipairs({ 'enable', 'disable', 'counts' }) do
    box.schema.func.create('audit.' .. name, { language = 'C', if_not_exists = true })
end
local function call(name, ...)
    return box.func['audit.' .. name]:call({ ... })
end

call('enable', 'stock')
stock:insert({ 1, 5 })
stock:replace({ 1, 7 })
stock:update(1, { { '-', 2, 10 } })    -- error: NegativeQty
stock:get(1)[2]                        -- 7
stock:delete(1)
call('counts')                         -- {inserts = 1, replaces = 1, updates = 0, deletes = 1}
call('disable')
stock:insert({ 2, -1 })                -- [2, -1]

docs.title: Writes to a space
docs.text:
trigger.onReplace(space_id, context, f) registers f as an on_replace trigger of the space, as space:on_replace(f) does in Lua. It runs for every insert, replace, update, delete and upsert, before the write is final, until remove() on the SpaceTrigger it returns.

f(context, event) gets a trigger.ReplaceEvent:

Field Is old the tuple before the write, or null for an insert new the tuple after it, or null for a delete space the name of the space, valid during f op .insert, .replace, .update, .delete or .upsert

The tuples are valid during f; copy what you keep.

An error returned by f rejects the statement: the write that fired the trigger fails with the error, as NegativeQty above. Within an explicit transaction only that statement is undone; the transaction goes on. error.BoxOp fails it with the message of Tarantool.

context is a pointer that must stay valid until remove(): a global, or memory you free after remove(), never a variable on the stack of the procedure that registers the trigger.

The trigger lives in the memory of the instance, not in the schema: it is gone after a restart. A module that needs it registers it again at startup, from a procedure called in the init script.

docs.title: Commit and rollback
docs.text: trigger.onCommit(context, f) and trigger.onRollback(context, f) run f(context) once, when the active transaction commits or rolls back. Transactions shows them.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
trigger.onShutdown(context, f) runs f(context) when the server shuts down gracefully, as box.ctl.on_shutdown does. trigger.removeShutdown(context, f) with the same pair removes it. audit logs its counts at shutdown:

I> audit: 1 inserts, 1 deletes

docs.title: The Lua state
docs.text: The triggers of a space and of a transaction have no C API in Tarantool: the SDK registers them through Lua, on the Lua state of the instance. A module cannot register them from a worker thread of coio.call, which has no Lua.

docs.title: Using with tt
docs.text: tt builds a Zig component of a package with its zig backend: it runs zig build of the component, takes the module and the program the build installs, and puts them into .rocks/ of the project, where Tarantool, tt run, tt test and the instances of the project find them, and into the archive of tt package pack. This page covers what that build does and how to set it up. Your first modules with tt walks through a first one.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
What Where it comes from tt 3 with the zig backend the standard module build of tt: tt version --modules lists build in a tt that has it Zig yours to install, see Install; tt looks for zig in .tarantool/bin of the project first, then on PATH Tarantool 3.5 or later tt binary install tarantool installs it into the project

tt does not install Zig. To pin the Zig of a project, link it into .tarantool/bin:

mkdir -p .tarantool/bin
ln -s /path/to/zig-0.17.1/zig .tarantool/bin/zig

docs.title: The build block
docs.text:
[components.hello]
path = "libs/hello"
exclude = ["zig-pkg/**"]

[components.hello.build]
backend = "zig"
module = "hello"
bin = "hello-client"

path is the directory of the component, where its build.zig and build.zig.zon are. tt runs there:

zig build -p _build/component/hello/zig-out --cache-dir _build/component/hello/zig-cache --release=safe

The build installs into a prefix of its own and keeps the cache of Zig there, under _build/ of the project, out of the sources. tt -V package build shows the line it runs.

Field Is module the module the build makes: tt takes lib/<module>.so (.dylib on macOS) from the prefix, as installModule installs it, or lib/lib<module>.so as b.installArtifact does bin the program the build makes: tt takes bin/<bin> from the prefix, as b.installArtifact installs it steps the steps of zig build to run, its default step by default: steps = ["modules"] for a build.zig that installs the module from a step of its own optimize Debug, ReleaseSafe, ReleaseFast or ReleaseSmall; ReleaseSafe by default. tt passes --release=safe, fast or small, and no flag for Debug, which the standardOptimizeOption of the build.zig takes options the options the build.zig declares with b.option, as strings: options = { tls = "true" } passes -Dtls=true incremental true skips zig build when the block, the files of the component, the version of Zig, build.zig and build.zig.zon are those of the last build static true checks that the program needs no shared library and the module none but the C library

A block names module, bin or both; one with neither is an error.

exclude = ["zig-pkg/**"] belongs to the component, not to the build. Zig fetches the dependencies of build.zig.zon into zig-pkg/ next to it, and tt lays out the *.lua files of a component into the package: without the exclude, the .lua files of zig-tarantool, those of its examples, end up in .rocks/share/tarantool/<namespace>/zig-pkg/ and in the archive.

docs.title: Where the files go
docs.text:
What Into the module .rocks/lib/tarantool/<namespace>/<module>.so the program .rocks/bin/<bin> a *.lua file of the component .rocks/share/tarantool/<namespace>/<path in the component>

The namespace is the name of the package unless the component sets namespace. A module named hello of the package myapp is myapp/hello.so, so its names carry myapp:

From The name In Zig Lua require('myapp.hello') lua.exportModule("myapp_hello", ...): dots become _ in luaopen_<name> a stored procedure box.schema.func.create('myapp.hello.add', {language = 'C'}) proc.exportProc("add", ...): Tarantool loads the module named up to the last dot, myapp.hello, and calls its symbol add

With namespace = "" the module is .rocks/lib/tarantool/hello.so, and the names are require('hello'), luaopen_hello and hello.add.

A dotted module, module = "codec.fast" for a build.zig that names it codec.fast, is lib/codec/fast.so of the prefix, as installModule installs it, and .rocks/lib/tarantool/myapp/codec/fast.so: require('myapp.codec.fast'), exported as myapp_codec_fast.

docs.title: A program next to the module
docs.text:
The same build.zig builds a program over the network client with addExecutable:

libs/hello/build.zig:

const std = @import("std");
const tarantool = @import("tarantool");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    const hello = tarantool.addModule(b, .{
        .name = "hello",
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/hello.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    tarantool.installModule(b, hello);

    const cli = tarantool.addExecutable(b, .{
        .name = "hello-client",
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/client.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    b.installArtifact(cli);
}

libs/hello/src/client.zig:

//! hello-client: call myapp.hello.add over the network.

const std = @import("std");
const client = @import("tarantool-client");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var conn = try client.Connection.connect(init.gpa, init.io, .{
        .address = "127.0.0.1:3301",
    });
    defer conn.close();

    const sum = try conn.call("myapp.hello.add", .{ 20, 22 }, i64);
    std.debug.print("myapp.hello.add(20, 22) = {d}\n", .{sum});
}

bin = "hello-client" in the block takes the program into .rocks/bin/.

docs.title: Run it in an instance
docs.text:
An instance of the project loads the module as the code of the project does. The code of the application is a component of Lua files, app/, which tt lays out into .rocks/share/tarantool/myapp/:

[components.app]
path = "app"

app/init.lua, the module myapp, declares the function and lets the guest call it:

box.schema.func.create('myapp.hello.add', {language = 'C', if_not_exists = true})
box.schema.user.grant('guest', 'execute', 'function', 'myapp.hello.add',
    {if_not_exists = true})

.templates/default/config.yaml runs one instance with it:

app:
  module: myapp

groups:
  group-001:
    replicasets:
      replicaset-001:
        instances:
          instance-001:
            iproto:
              listen:
              - uri: 127.0.0.1:3301

$ tt package build
$ tt instance start
   • Starting an instance [myapp:instance-001]...
$ .rocks/bin/hello-client
myapp.hello.add(20, 22) = 42
$ tt instance stop --yes

docs.title: zig-tarantool from a checkout
docs.text:
While you change zig-tarantool and the project together, depend on a checkout of it instead of a commit. The path is relative to the component: for a checkout next to the project, zig-tarantool/ beside myapp/, libs/hello/build.zig.zon has

.dependencies = .{
    .tarantool = .{ .path = "../../../zig-tarantool" },
},

An incremental build does not see a change of the checkout, which is outside the component: tt package build --rebuild builds anyway.

docs.title: Pack and install
docs.text:
$ tt package pack
/home/me/myapp/_build/pack/myapp-1.0.0-linux-amd64.tt

The archive carries the module and the program, built for the machine it is packed on, and an installed version of the package loads and runs them as the project does. The module links against the C library of that machine: pack on the oldest system the package runs on. static = true checks that the module needs no other shared library; a program of addExecutable links no C library and needs none.

Zig fetches the dependencies of build.zig.zon itself, as it builds: tt package fetch does not run the build, and the lock of tt does not pin them. The .hash of each dependency in build.zig.zon does.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
• The build installed no module. tt names what the build did install:
$ tt package build
   ⨯ building component "hello": zig build installed no module "hullo": .../_build/component/hello/zig-out/lib has none of hullo.so, hullo.dylib, libhullo.so, libhullo.dylib (it installed hello.so); install it with installModule of zig-tarantool, or name the step that installs it in steps

module and the .name of addModule must be the same name. - A module renamed is still in .rocks/. A build keeps what an earlier build of the component made while the file is there: after a change of module, tt package build --rebuild drops the old one. - undefined symbol: box_... on require or on the first call. The Tarantool is older than 3.5, see Install. - undefined symbol: luaopen_myapp_hello on require('myapp.hello'). The name given to exportModule does not match the path of the module: it is myapp_hello for myapp/hello.so.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text: What does not work yet, or works in a way that may surprise you. Open work is tracked in the GitHub issues.

docs.title: Platforms and versions
docs.text:
• Modules need Tarantool 3.5. On 3.0 to 3.4 a module fails to load with an undefined symbol, such as box_tuple_data. The network client works with 3.0 and later.
  • macOS is tested against one Tarantool. Homebrew has one version of Tarantool, so CI runs the suite on macOS against that one; macOS on Intel is built, not run.
  • No releases. The package has no versions; depend on a commit.

docs.title: Stored procedures and Lua functions
docs.text:
• An integer does not decode into a float. An f64 parameter fails with NotFloat on 1, and Lua sends every whole number as an integer, 1.0 included. Pass a fraction, or take the argument as a msgpack.Value in a raw procedure. Lua functions of lua.exportModule are not affected: they read Lua numbers.
  • A typed procedure loses the message of Tarantool. A typed procedure that returns error.BoxOp fails with the message BoxOp; a raw procedure and a Lua function report the message Tarantool set.
  • Arguments have an exact arity. An optional parameter still takes an argument: pass box.NULL, since a nil at the end of a Lua table is not in it.
  • Slices do not decode. A typed procedure cannot take []T other than a string; a Lua function can.

docs.title: The box API
docs.text:
• No DDL. There is no API to create spaces or indexes: do it in Lua (#8).
  • No Index.deleteRange of Tarantool 3.9 yet (#3).
  • Triggers go through Lua. The triggers of spaces and transactions are registered on the Lua state of the instance, since the C API has none.

docs.title: The network client
docs.text:
• The address is an IP address. host:port takes a numeric host; resolve names first.
  • Only chap-sha1. No pap-sha256 and no TLS (#2).
  • No SQL (#6) and no pagination of select (#7).
  • One request at a time. A connection waits for each reply; use a Batch to send several. Two fibers or threads must not share a connection without a lock.
  • No background reader. Watcher events arrive only while you call into the connection (#15).
  • Streams take no options. begin sends no isolation level or timeout, and calls and batches cannot join a stream (#14).
  • Index handles read only. space.index(name) has get and select; an update or a delete goes through the primary key.
  • decodeRow takes one tuple. It needs the MessagePack of a single tuple, while the raw requests return the array of the reply.

docs.title: Inside Tarantool
docs.text:
• fiberio.io() does the network only. Files, timers, async and the rest of std.Io panic with the name of the operation. An evented std.Io example is open work (#1).
  • symresolve needs a symbol table. On a stripped executable it resolves nothing.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page describes how the package is tested: the unit tests, the luatest suite that runs modules and programs against a live Tarantool, the check of the C API, CI and coverage. It is for those who change the package.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Path Holds Run by src/**/*.zig, test/*.zig unit tests: the codec, the protocol, the client, the update operations zig build test test/integration/<name>.zig test modules, built to <name>.so zig build integration examples/<name>/<name>.zig the examples, built to <name>.so zig build integration test/client/<name>.zig test programs of the network client, built to bin/<name> zig build integration test/luatest/<name>_test.lua the luatest groups that load those modules and run those programs zig build integration examples/consumer/ a project that depends on this one zig build consumer

The build finds the files of test/integration, examples and test/client by listing the directories, so a new file is built without a change to build.zig.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
The unit tests need nothing but Zig:

zig build test

The luatest suite needs tarantool 3.5 or later on PATH, and luatest, which deps.sh installs into .rocks/ with tt:

./deps.sh                 # once; TT=/path/to/tt ./deps.sh if tt is not on PATH
zig build integration

Each group starts a Tarantool of its own with luatest.Server, with zig-out/lib on its package.cpath. To run one group:

zig build modules
LUA_PATH="./test/luatest/?.lua;;$LUA_PATH" ./.rocks/bin/luatest test/luatest/kv_test.lua

In the tarantool/tarantool Docker images, unset TT_APP_NAME and TT_INSTANCE_NAME first: the images set them, and they make every Tarantool the tests start wait for a cluster configuration.

docs.title: Add a test
docs.text:
• Box API: a module in test/integration/<name>.zig, and a group in test/luatest/<name>_test.lua that creates its functions and calls them.
  • Network client: a program in test/client/<name>.zig that prints TAP and exits with a non-zero code on failure, and a case in test/luatest/client_test.lua that runs it with TT_URI, TT_USER and TT_PASS set.
  • An example: examples/<name>/<name>.zig, with its group in test/luatest/<name>_test.lua.

docs.title: Check the C API
docs.text:
tarantool.c declares the C API of Tarantool by hand. To check it against the headers of an installed Tarantool:

zig build verify-cabi -Dverify-cabi=true

It translates module.h with translate-c and compares the type of every declared function, and the value of every constant, with it at compile time. It reads /usr/include/tarantool, /opt/homebrew/include/tarantool on macOS, or the directory of -Dtarantool-include=<dir>.

docs.title: Check the module boundaries
docs.text:
zig build purity

compiles small programs in which tarantool-client or tarantool-proto imports tarantool, and passes when each of them fails to compile. See Modules and layers.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml runs on every push and pull request, and weekly:

Job Does build zig fmt --check, the unit tests, purity, consumer, a build of the modules for aarch64-linux, aarch64-macos and x86_64-macos, and a ReleaseFast build integration on Linux x86_64 with Tarantool 3.5 to 3.9, on Linux arm64 with 3.5 and 3.9, on macOS with the Tarantool of Homebrew: the unit tests, verify-cabi against the installed headers, then the luatest suite doc-examples the examples of this documentation, below, on 3.5 and 3.9 coverage the coverage report, below, on 3.9

The jobs run on the runners themselves, with no container: .github/actions/tarantool installs Tarantool and its headers with tarantool/setup-tarantool on Linux, which takes the latest release of a series, and with Homebrew on macOS, and installs tt. The weekly run tests the new releases. Dependabot keeps the actions, pinned by commit, up to date.

.github/workflows/docs.yml builds this documentation with ci/docs.py build, which fails on a broken link or a page missing from the nav, and publishes it, see Versions and publishing.

docs.title: The examples of the documentation
docs.text:
python3 ci/doc_examples.py [page ...]

builds the examples of doc/ and runs them against the tarantool on PATH. A file a page shows, a line `src/name.zig`: and a block after it, goes into a project of the page in zig-out/doc-examples/<page>/, which depends on this repository. Then:

  • the Lua blocks of the page run as one script, and every line expression -- result must give the result;
  • a .lua file that listens on a port is started as a server;
  • the tarantool file.lua and ./zig-out/bin/name commands of a console block must print the lines that follow them.

So an example that stops building, or a result that changes, fails CI. Write examples that way: label each file, end each call with the result it gives.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
ci/coverage.sh <out-dir>

measures the line coverage of src/ with kcov, over the unit tests, every Tarantool the luatest suite starts, and the test programs. It replaces /usr/bin/tarantool with a wrapper that runs it under kcov, so run it on a throwaway machine: a CI runner, or a container of tarantool/tarantool with kcov installed and --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE. It writes <out-dir>/merged/index.html and a summary by file, <out-dir>/summary.md. The coverage job of CI uploads both.

zig build test -Dllvm -Dcoverage=<dir> covers the unit tests alone. kcov reads the debug information that the LLVM backend emits; -Dllvm selects it.

docs.title: The documentation
docs.text:
python3 -m pip install -r doc/requirements.txt
python3 ci/docs.py serve            # or: ci/docs.py serve --lang ru

serves the guides with live reload on http://127.0.0.1:8000/, both languages, the Russian pages under /ru/, and the API reference under /api/.

The site has two parts:

  • the guides, doc/**/*.md, written by hand and built by mkdocs, in English and Russian;
  • the API reference, which zig build docs generates from the doc comments of src/ with the autodoc of Zig. A doc comment is the reference: change the comment, not a page.

docs.title: Versions and publishing
docs.text:
The published site keeps every version, on the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves:

Path Is / a redirect to /en/ /en/, /ru/ a redirect to the default version of the language /en/<version>/, /ru/<version>/ the guides of a version /api/, /api/<version>/ the API reference, the same way /<lang>/versions.json, /api/versions.json the versions, which the version selector of the guides reads

A version is master, published on every push to it, or a release: the tag v1.2.0 publishes 1.2.0. The highest release is aliased latest, which is the default; before the first release, the default is master. A release on an older line, v1.1.5 after v1.2.0, does not take latest.

The documentation of a release is fixed on a branch doc/<tag>, by convention: branch doc/v1.2.0 off the tag v1.2.0, commit the fix there and push it. A push to doc/v1.2.0 publishes 1.2.0 again, keeping its aliases. Merge the fix to master too, so that the next release has it.

git switch -c doc/v1.2.0 v1.2.0
# fix doc/, commit
git push origin doc/v1.2.0

python3 ci/docs.py deploy master                # publish to the local gh-pages
python3 ci/docs.py deploy v1.2.0 --push         # what CI does for a tag
python3 ci/docs.py build                        # one version into site/, as CI checks it

mike publishes the guides: each language is a separate build, mike deploy --deploy-prefix <lang>, and Material's version selector reads the versions.json it writes. ci/docs.py adds the API reference and the root redirects in the same layout. The language switcher links the same page in the other language of the same version (doc/overrides/partials/alternate.html). Only the top of ci/docs.py, which builds the API reference, is specific to this project; the rest of the publishing can serve any mkdocs project with a reference generated next to it.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text:
A translation of doc/<page>.md is doc/<page>.ru.md, next to it, with the same headings in the same order and links to the same .md files: the site sends a link to the translation when there is one. A page with no translation shows the English one, so pages can be translated one at a time. A new section of the nav needs its Russian title under nav_translations in mkdocs.yml.

python3 ci/doc_translations.py

lists the translations whose English page changed after them, with the commits to follow, and those whose English page is gone. docs.yml runs it as a warning.

docs.title: API by module

docs.title: Build reference
docs.text: The build.zig of zig-tarantool exports helpers for the build.zig of a project that depends on it, and defines the steps that build and test the package itself. This page lists both.

docs.title: Helpers
docs.text:
A project calls them with the package imported under the name it has in build.zig.zon, which must be tarantool:

const tarantool = @import("tarantool");

The helpers find the package among the dependencies of the project themselves, and build it for the target and optimize they are given: the project does not call b.dependency.

docs.title: addModule
docs.text:
pub fn addModule(b: *std.Build, options: ModuleOptions) *std.Build.Step.Compile

Creates a Tarantool module: a shared library that Tarantool loads, for box.schema.func.create('<name>.<symbol>', {language = 'C'}) or for require('<name>'). Its root source file can import tarantool, tarantool-client, tarantool-proto and msgpack. The symbols of Tarantool stay undefined, for Tarantool to resolve when it loads the library.

Option Is .name the name of the module; a dotted name a.b installs as a/b.so .root_source_file its root source file .target, .optimize as for any compile step .imports more imports, on top of the four above

It returns the compile step, which you can change further: link a C library, add an include path.

docs.title: installModule, addInstallModule
docs.text:
pub fn installModule(b: *std.Build, lib: *std.Build.Step.Compile) void
pub fn addInstallModule(b: *std.Build, lib: *std.Build.Step.Compile) *std.Build.Step.InstallArtifact

installModule installs a module as lib/<name>.so, or lib/<name>.dylib when the target is macOS, under the install prefix, as part of zig build. addInstallModule makes the same install step without adding it to zig build, for a step of your own.

Do not install a module with b.installArtifact: it names the file lib<name>.so, and Tarantool looks for <name>.so.

docs.title: addExecutable
docs.text:
pub fn addExecutable(b: *std.Build, options: ExecutableOptions) *std.Build.Step.Compile

Creates a program that can import tarantool-client, tarantool-proto and msgpack, with the same options as addModule. It cannot import tarantool, which only runs inside Tarantool. Install it with b.installArtifact, into bin/.

docs.title: moduleExtension
docs.text:
pub fn moduleExtension(target: std.Target) []const u8

"dylib" for macOS, "so" for the other systems: the extension Tarantool looks for. In Lua, require('tarantool').build.mod_format says the same.

docs.title: Loading a module
docs.text:
Tarantool looks for a module on package.cpath, as Lua does:

local ext = require('tarantool').build.mod_format
package.cpath = '/path/to/zig-out/lib/?.' .. ext .. ';' .. package.cpath

Without that, it also looks in the current directory, and in .rocks/lib/tarantool/ of the current directory and of its parents, so copying the module there works as well. A tt package puts it there: see Using with tt.

zig build -p <prefix> installs into <prefix>/lib and <prefix>/bin instead of zig-out. zig build -Dtarget=aarch64-macos cross-compiles the modules and programs, if the project passes b.standardTargetOptions to the helpers.

docs.title: Steps of this repository
docs.text:
Step Does zig build test the unit tests: the codec, the protocol, the client, the update operations; no Tarantool needed zig build modules builds the examples, the test modules and the test programs zig build integration builds them, then runs the luatest suite against tarantool on PATH zig build consumer builds examples/consumer, a project that uses the helpers, and checks what it installed zig build purity checks that tarantool-client and tarantool-proto cannot import tarantool: their compilation must fail zig build verify-cabi -Dverify-cabi=true checks the declarations of tarantool.c against the module.h of an installed Tarantool zig build docs generates the API reference from the doc comments into zig-out/docs/api/; see Testing Option Does -Dtarantool-include=<dir> where verify-cabi reads module.h; /usr/include/tarantool by default, /opt/homebrew/include/tarantool on macOS -Dllvm builds with the LLVM backend, which kcov needs -Dcoverage=<dir> runs the unit tests under kcov, writing the reports to <dir>

Testing describes the suite.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The SDK reports failures as Zig errors, and turns them into errors of Tarantool or Lua at the boundary. This page lists the errors by module, and what the caller of a procedure, of a Lua function or of a client request sees.

docs.title: What the caller sees
docs.text:
Where the Zig error comes from The caller gets a typed procedure, exportProc a ClientError, code 102 (ER_PROC_C), with the name of the error as the message a raw procedure, exportRaw, returning error.BoxOp the error Tarantool set, with its own type, code and message a raw procedure returning another error a ClientError 102 with the name of the error proc.fail(err, message) as above, with message instead of the name err.setBoxError(code, message) and return -1 a ClientError with that code and message a Lua function of lua.exportModule a Lua error: the message of Tarantool for error.BoxOp, the name of the error otherwise an on_replace trigger the same, as the error of the statement that fired it

A typed procedure reports error.BoxOp as BoxOp, without the message of Tarantool; write a raw procedure to keep it. In Lua, the error object has the fields type, code and message:

local ok, e = pcall(box.func['procs.clamp'].call, box.func['procs.clamp'], { 1, 10, 0 })
e.code     -- 102
e.message  -- EmptyRange

docs.title: The error of Tarantool
docs.text:
When a box operation fails, Tarantool sets the error of the fiber and the SDK returns error.BoxOp. tarantool.err reads and sets that error:

Function Does lastError() the error, as BoxError{ code, message, type }, or null; its strings are valid until the next box call lastMessage(&buf) copies the message into buf, and returns the copy, or null setBoxError(code, message) sets the error; the message is cut at 256 bytes

An error that is not error.BoxOp comes from the SDK, and the error of Tarantool may be one left over from an earlier operation: read it only after BoxOp.

docs.title: Errors by module
docs.text: Module Errors box NoSuchSpace, NoSuchIndex: the name does not exist; BoxOp: Tarantool failed the operation tuple NewFailed, UpdateFailed, NullTupleData txn BoxOp; NoTxn: no active transaction; StaleSavepoint: the savepoint belongs to another transaction; TxnStarted: the isolation is set after the first write; OutOfMemory seq SeqOp: Tarantool failed the operation; NoSuchSequence keydef KeyDefFailed, ExtractFailed fiber FiberOp: the fiber was not created fiber.Channel InvalidCapacity, Closed, Cancelled cond CondOp, Timeout, Cancelled latch LatchOp coio Timeout, CoioOp; OffloadFailed from call; Timeout, ResolveFailed from getAddrInfo box.info.waitRo Timeout, Cancelled trigger TriggerOp: the registration failed; NoTxn decimal DecimalError: the operation failed; InvalidDecimal: not a decimal; Overflow: out of the integer range lua, the typed functions ArityMismatch, TypeMismatch, Overflow, and the errors of the function proc, the typed procedures wrong argument count, and the errors of decoding

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
msgpack.DecodeError, from msgpack.decode, from the arguments of a typed procedure, and from the results of the client:

Error The input NotInt, NotBool, NotFloat, NotStr, NotBin, NotArray, NotMap, NotExt has another type Overflow is an integer out of the range of the type ArityMismatch is an array of another length UnknownField, MissingField is a map with a key that is no field, or without one that is Truncated ends in the middle of a value InvalidExt is an extension whose payload is not valid for the type OutOfMemory needed memory for a dynamic value, and there was none

docs.title: The network client
docs.text:
client.Error, plus the errors of decoding and of the socket:

Error Means The connection ServerError the server refused the request; conn.last_error has the details usable AuthFailed the login failed closed by connect MoreThanOne get matched several tuples usable UnsupportedServer the server lacks a feature the client needs, such as Tarantool before 3.0 closed by connect InvalidAddress the address is not host:port with a numeric host not opened ConnectionClosed, ReadFailed, WriteFailed the connection broke close it ProtocolError the reply violates the protocol close it

connect also returns the errors of std.Io.net for the socket, such as ConnectionRefused and Timeout.
